digest:
/ — Computer science, explained until it actually makes sense
  sections: Labs, extras and revision; B · Computational thinking and programming; How to use this

/a/a1/boolean-algebra/ — Truth tables and Boolean algebra (A1.2.7)
  Writing down everything a circuit does, then finding a smaller circuit that does exactly the same thing.
  sections: Building a truth table; From table to expression; The laws; De Morgan's laws; Simplifying, worked

/a/a1/compression/ — Compression (A1.2.5)
  Making a file smaller by writing the same thing more cleverly, or by deciding some of it was not worth keeping.
  sections: Lossless; Lossy

/a/a1/fetch-decode-execute/ — The fetch–decode–execute cycle (A1.1.3)
  The loop the processor has been running since you turned the machine on, traced register by register until there is nothing mysterious left in it.
  sections: Fetch; Decode; Execute; Watch it run; Clock speed, and why it lies

/a/a1/images-and-sound/ — Images and sound (A1.2.4)
  Turning something continuous — a scene, a pressure wave — into a finite list of numbers, and what is unavoidably lost in the process.
  sections: Bitmap images; Sound; Nyquist, and the number 44,100; Quantisation error

/a/a1/inside-the-processor/ — Inside the processor (A1.1.2)
  The four parts every CPU has, what each one is physically for, and why the design has barely changed in eighty years.
  sections: The four parts; The registers worth naming; The three buses; Why this design, and why it has lasted

/a/a1/karnaugh-maps/ — Karnaugh maps (A1.2.8)
  A way of simplifying Boolean expressions by looking rather than by algebra, and the reason its rows are numbered so strangely.
  sections: The layout, and why it is odd; Grouping; Reading a group; Don't-care conditions; Prime implicants; Where maps run out

/a/a1/logic-circuits/ — Building real circuits (A1.2.9)
  Adders, multiplexers, decoders and the first circuit that can remember something — plus what happens in the nanoseconds before a circuit settles.
  sections: The half adder; The full adder; Multiplexers and decoders; Memory: the SR latch; Delay and hazards

/a/a1/logic-gates/ — Logic gates (A1.2.6)
  The seven switches everything else is built from, what each one physically does, and why two of them could do the whole job alone.
  sections: AND; OR; NOT; NAND and NOR; XOR and XNOR; Universality; Reading a circuit

/a/a1/memory-hierarchy/ — Primary memory and the hierarchy (A1.1.4)
  Why a computer has five kinds of memory instead of one good one, and why the answer is economics rather than engineering.
  sections: Primary memory: what the CPU can reach; The hierarchy, level by level; Cache, and why it works at all; Virtual memory

/a/a1/negative-numbers/ — Negative numbers and two's complement (A1.2.2)
  How to write a minus sign using only zeros and ones, and why the obvious method was abandoned for a stranger one that makes subtraction free.
  sections: The obvious method, and why it fails; Two's complement; Reading one back; Why hardware designers chose it; The lopsided range; Overflow; Shifts

/a/a1/number-bases/ — Binary, denary and hexadecimal (A1.2.1)
  Counting in a base other than ten, why machines count in two, and why programmers write in sixteen.
  sections: What a base actually means; Binary; Hexadecimal; How much can $n$ bits hold?; The units problem

/a/a1/operating-systems/ — What an operating system does (A1.3.1)
  The program whose job is to stop every other program from having to know how the machine works — and from wrecking each other.
  sections: Program, process, thread; Managing the processor; Managing memory; Managing files; Kernel mode and user mode

/a/a1/scheduling/ — Scheduling and interrupts (A1.3.2)
  Deciding which process runs next, why every fair answer is unfair to somebody, and how the machine gets interrupted mid-sentence.
  sections: First come first served; Shortest job first; Round robin; Priority and starvation; Interrupts

/a/a1/text-and-characters/ — Representing text (A1.2.3)
  How letters became numbers, why that nearly broke the internet for most of the world, and how Unicode fixed it.
  sections: ASCII; Unicode; UTF-8; What it costs

/a/a1/translators/ — Translators (A1.4.1)
  Getting from something a person can read to something a processor can execute, and the two very different bargains available for doing it.
  sections: The layers; Compilers and interpreters; Inside a compiler; Bytecode, and the middle way

/a/a1/what-a-computer-is/ — What a computer actually is (A1.1.1)
  Before any of the detail, the one idea the whole subject rests on — a machine that stores its own instructions and follows them without understanding them.
  sections: Start with what a machine can do; The stored-program idea; The machine does not understand anything; Why everything is two states; The four-part model; Hardware, software, and a blurred line

/a/a2/data-transmission/ — Data transmission and security (A2.3.1)
  Chopping a message into pieces, sending them by different routes, checking they survived, and stopping anyone reading them on the way.
  sections: Packets; Circuit versus packet switching; Bandwidth and latency; Detecting errors; Encryption

/a/a2/network-architecture/ — Topologies and architectures (A2.2.1)
  How machines are physically arranged, who is in charge once they are, and what breaks when one of them fails.
  sections: Topologies; The boxes in between; Architectures; Cloud

/a/a2/networks-and-protocols/ — Networks and protocols (A2.1.1)
  What has to be agreed before two machines can say anything to each other, and why those agreements are stacked in layers.
  sections: Networks by size; Layers; Encapsulation; Addresses

/a/a3/normalisation/ — Normalisation (A3.1.2)
  A procedure for splitting tables until every fact sits in exactly one place, and the reasons you might deliberately stop short.
  sections: Functional dependency; First normal form; Second normal form; Third normal form; When not to normalise

/a/a3/relational-model/ — The relational model (A3.1.1)
  Why data is split across many tables rather than kept in one big one, and what the keys are actually holding together.
  sections: Why one table fails; Keys; Relationships

/a/a3/sql/ — Querying with SQL (A3.1.3)
  Saying what you want rather than how to fetch it, and the handful of clauses that cover almost every question anyone asks of a database.
  sections: The shape of a query; Joins; Aggregates and grouping; Changing data; SQL injection

/a/a3/transactions/ — Transactions and other kinds of database (A3.2.1 HL)
  Making several changes count as one, what happens when two people change the same row at once, and when the relational model is the wrong tool.
  sections: Transactions; ACID; What isolation protects you from; When relational is the wrong model

/a/a4/neural-networks-and-ethics/ — Neural networks, bias and responsibility (A4.1.4 HL)
  What a neuron actually computes, why depth helps, and the ways a technically correct model can still do harm.
  sections: One neuron; Why the activation function is not optional; Training; Bias; Responsibility

/a/a4/supervised-learning/ — Supervised learning and how it fails (A4.1.2)
  Classification, regression, and the two ways a model can be wrong that have nothing to do with the algorithm being bad.
  sections: Two shapes of problem; Training, validation, test; Overfitting; Measuring properly

/a/a4/unsupervised-learning/ — Unsupervised learning (A4.1.3)
  Finding structure nobody labelled, why there is no right answer to check against, and how k-means actually works.
  sections: Clustering; k-means; Choosing k; Scaling matters

/a/a4/what-machine-learning-is/ — What machine learning is (A4.1.1)
  Programs that are not written but fitted, why anyone would want that, and the three ways of learning you are expected to tell apart.
  sections: What is actually being learned; The three kinds; The vocabulary
